checkpoints: Severity of the leak is very high: DO has no permission boundary or assume-role like AWS, so control-plane rights live entirely in the single full-access PAT's scope, not in a `.tf` resource — leaking it means losing the ability to create/delete every Droplet, VPC, project, and database in the account.
Core redesign principle: since there's no DO policy layer to write (no IAM-style fine-grained policy), separate credentials by need/job-function instead of by policy.
Read-only jobs (lint, scan, cost report) should use a dedicated read-only PAT, so even if it leaks it can't create or delete anything.
Write jobs (Terraform apply, deploy) should use a separate write PAT, stored in the CI's secret manager, never committed to the repo, and rotated on a schedule.
For Spaces, issue per-bucket Spaces keys scoped to read/readwrite instead of fullaccess, kept entirely separate from the PAT.
For Managed Database, don't route access through the PAT at all — use a dedicated DB user plus a firewall trusted-source per service.
Because DO has no automatic IAM audit tooling (no Access Analyzer equivalent), existing tokens and their scopes must be periodically reviewed manually via the control panel or API.

Be honest with the manager that AWS-style defense-in-depth isn't achievable on DO; the real risk reduction comes from minimizing the number of jobs holding high-privilege tokens, shortening token lifetimes, and separating credentials along the right resource boundaries (control-plane / object storage / database) rather than relying on an automatic guardrail to cap blast radius.

Choosing a flavor on DigitalOcean means changing a single argument, `size` — the slug itself already encodes the full spec, and there is no "custom machine type" concept for freely picking CPU/RAM like on GCP; DO only offers fixed presets.
The `s-` prefix denotes Basic shared-CPU.
The `g-` prefix denotes General-Purpose, with a balanced vCPU:RAM ratio (~1 vCPU : 4 GB), the default choice when the workload is unclear.
The `c-` prefix denotes CPU-Optimized, with dedicated vCPU and a 1 vCPU : 2 GB ratio, meant for CPU-heavy workloads.
The `m-` prefix denotes Memory-Optimized, with a 1 vCPU : 8 GB ratio, meant for RAM-hungry workloads.
The `so-`/`gd-` prefix denotes Storage-Optimized, with large-capacity NVMe storage.
Picking the wrong flavor doesn't break anything functionally — it just wastes real money, since the CPU:RAM ratio it locks you into may not match the workload's actual bottleneck.

Matching principle, illustrated by a concrete case: a single-threaded Node.js event-loop backend is CPU-bound, so `g-4vcpu-8gb` General-Purpose wastes money paying for 8 GB RAM while using only ~1 GB — the right pick is `c-2`/`c-4` CPU-Optimized for dedicated vCPU; generally, CPU-bound workloads (Node.js, build server, video encoding) → CPU-Optimized, memory-bound (Redis, OLTP Postgres, JVM heap) → Memory-Optimized, disk-heavy (ClickHouse, Elasticsearch, data lake) → Storage-Optimized, balanced/unclear workload → General-Purpose.
Disagree with the teammate — simply upgrading the Droplet to a bigger size is not the right fix.
Upgrading the Droplet ties the disk tightly to CPU/RAM: needing more disk means swapping the whole Droplet flavor.
The disk remains the Droplet's boot disk, so it can't be backed up or migrated independently of the Droplet.
Use a Block Volume instead: a standalone resource, created ahead of time and attached later, with a lifecycle entirely decoupled from the Droplet.
A Volume can be detached and attached to a different Droplet, and can be snapshotted independently.
Unlike the boot disk — which disappears when the Droplet is destroyed — a Volume keeps existing (and keeps billing) even after the original Droplet has been destroyed.
Use a Volume for data that must persist across repeated Droplet re-creation, e.g. Postgres/MongoDB data directories, log file streaming, application working set.

Verify independence with `terraform output volume_attached_droplet_ids` (exactly one Droplet ID at a time, since Volumes are single-attach) and by confirming the Volume still exists/bills after the host Droplet is `terraform destroy`-ed.

Root cause: DO Volumes tie IOPS to the volume's allocated size — not to how full it actually is — instead of offering a separate provisioned-IOPS tier like AWS EBS io2 (which lets you tune IOPS independently of size, up to 64k IOPS on 100 GB); so a 100 GB volume that's only 30 GB full still gets exactly the IOPS tied to its full 100 GB allocation.
Dev/test never surfaced the problem because the lighter workload never hit that IOPS ceiling.
Production's write-heavy concurrent writes hit the IOPS ceiling, and that throttling is what shows up as the observed 50-200ms P99 write latency spikes.
Fix 1: increase the volume's size — even without needing more storage capacity — to buy higher IOPS, accepting the extra cost (~$0.10/GiB/month), scaling up until the target IOPS is reached.
Fix 2: if increasing size still isn't enough, move entirely to a DO Managed Database (tuned specifically for databases) instead of continuing to inflate a self-managed Droplet's volume.

Root cause of the 422 error: both `digitalocean_volume_attachment` resources point to the same `volume_id`, but DigitalOcean Block Volumes are single-attach — only one Droplet can be attached at a time, so the second attachment attempt is rejected.

This single-attach behavior is a hard constraint of the DO Volume service itself, not a Terraform limitation — contrasted with AWS EBS io2 Multi-Attach, which allows up to 16 EC2 instances to attach the same volume.

Technical reason for single-attach: block storage assumes a single writer, since typical filesystem journals (ext4/xfs) aren't safe with multiple simultaneous writers without a dedicated cluster filesystem (e.g. OCFS2, GFS2).
Alternative architecture option 1: use Spaces (S3-compatible object storage) when it's static assets/files that multiple workers need to read.

Alternative architecture option 2: stand up a dedicated NFS server (a Droplet exporting a directory over NFS) when a real shared filesystem is needed, accepting it as a DIY solution that is slower than local block storage.
Verification for the Spaces path: both workers must be able to read/write via the S3 API without errors.

Verification for the single-attach Volume path (dropping the other attachment resource, keeping the Volume for just one worker): `terraform output volume_attached_droplet_ids` must return exactly one Droplet ID.

Root issue: the LB is attached via hardcoded `droplet_ids = [api_1.id, api_2.id]` (two fixed Droplet IDs), completely disconnected from the actual backend — a `digitalocean_droplet_autoscale` pool with `min_instances = 2`/`max_instances = 6`; the LB only ever serves the exact two Droplets declared at write time.

Scale-out failure: when the pool creates a new node because CPU exceeds `target_cpu_utilization = 0.6`, that node is invisible to the LB (not in the hardcoded ID list) and gets zero traffic — autoscaling out is effectively meaningless.
Scale-in failure: when the pool removes a node, the LB keeps routing traffic to a Droplet that no longer exists, causing failed requests.
Fix: replace `droplet_ids` with `droplet_tag = "api"`, matching the `tags = ["api"]` already declared in `droplet_template`, so the LB selects backends by tag instead of fixed IDs.
Benefit of the fix: every node the pool spawns automatically carries the `api` tag and falls into the LB's scope the moment it's created, with no need to edit the LB config on every scale event.

Verification: deliberately increase load to trigger scale-out, then confirm `doctl compute load-balancer get <id> --format DropletIDs` lists the current node count, or watch consecutive `curl` round-robin responses cycle through the newly created node.

Root cause: `cooldown_minutes = 1` is too low, so the pool never gets time to stabilize between scale events — any mild natural fluctuation in traffic around the target keeps triggering repeated add/remove cycles.

Secondary cause: `target_cpu_utilization = 0.5` / `target_memory_utilization = 0.5` sit close to the system's normal average load, so a slight traffic nudge up or down crosses the threshold and triggers scaling even though load is "fairly stable on average."
Fix: raise `cooldown_minutes` to a reasonable value (e.g. 5-10 minutes) to give the pool time to stabilize before another scale event is considered.
Fix: raise the target utilization (e.g. to around 0.6-0.7) to build in headroom before hitting the threshold, avoiding unnecessary scaling triggered by natural traffic variance.
Cost impact: flapping costs real money because every scale-out Droplet is billed hourly the moment it's created, even if it lives only a few minutes before being removed by scale-in.
Stability impact: flapping is also destabilizing because traffic can be routed to a node that is mid-creation or mid-removal.

Verification: after the fix, monitor `terraform output autoscale_current_utilization` and `doctl compute droplet list --tag-name <pool-tag>` over several hours — node count should stay stable around `min_instances` under normal load, rising only for a genuine traffic spike sustained long enough to clear the cooldown.

digitalocean_certificate with type "lets_encrypt" only needs name + domains — DO auto-issues via DNS challenge and auto-renews, unlike the custom type which needs private_key/leaf_certificate/certificate_chain.

The load balancer selects backends via droplet_tag = "api-pool" instead of droplet_ids, because the backend is an autoscale pool — every node the pool spawns carries this tag and automatically falls into the LB's scope.
The HTTPS:443 → HTTP:80 forwarding rule means the LB terminates TLS at the entry so backends only receive plain HTTP, reducing encryption CPU load on every node.
A parallel HTTP:80 → HTTP:80 forwarding rule is still kept alongside the HTTPS rule, because redirect_http_to_https = true needs an existing HTTP forwarding rule for the redirect to attach to.

The healthcheck pings /healthz every 10s (check_interval_seconds = 10) and removes a node after 3 consecutive failures (unhealthy_threshold = 3), asymmetric with healthy_threshold = 5 to avoid flapping a flaky node.

Let's Encrypt can only issue once the domain's DNS points to the LB's IP, so the correct order is: apply the LB first without the HTTPS forwarding rule/cert to get lb_ip via terraform output, point an A record api.example.com at that IP, wait for DNS to propagate, and only then apply the cert + HTTPS forwarding rule — applying everything in one pass while DNS isn't pointed correctly leaves the cert stuck pending.
Compare the exact `healthcheck.path` configured in Terraform (`"/"`) against the app's actual behavior at that specific path, rather than the `/healthz` path that was manually tested.
Reproduce exactly what the LB probe sends by running `curl -i http://localhost:8080/` (the health check's actual path, not `/healthz`).
Observe that this request returns `301 Moved Permanently` with `Location: /app/` instead of `200`.
Identify the root cause: DigitalOcean's LB health check only counts status `200` as healthy and does not auto-follow redirects, so a `301` is treated as a failure even though it is valid HTTP.
Rule out Cloud Firewall blocking probe traffic from the LB's internal subnet, since the local `curl` still returns a normal response — the problem is the response content, not a dropped connection.
Rule out an insufficient `response_timeout_seconds = 5`, since the response is near-instant.
Apply the correct fix: set `healthcheck { path = "/healthz" }` to match the endpoint that actually returns `200`.
Avoid the wrong fix of changing the app so `/` returns `200`, since the root redirect to `/app/` may be intentional routing behavior that should not be altered for health-check reasons.

Bucket ACL and object ACL are two independent levels with no automatic inheritance/sync between them — whether something on Spaces is public is decided by the combination of both layers together, not a single master switch controlling everything inside the bucket.
Spaces supports exactly two canned ACL values, `private` and `public-read`, a narrower set than S3 offers (no `authenticated-read`, no `aws-exec-read`, no canonical-id grantees).
The bucket itself carries its own ACL, set when the bucket is created (`digitalocean_spaces_bucket`), defaulting to `private`.
Each object also carries its own separate ACL, set at PUT time (`digitalocean_spaces_bucket_object`), also defaulting to `private` if unspecified.
When a bucket's ACL is `private` (e.g. bucket `assets`), it blocks public listing/reading of the bucket's contents by default.

An object explicitly uploaded with `acl = "public-read"` (e.g. `logo.png`) remains directly readable via its own URL (`bucket_domain_name/logo.png`) even though the parent bucket is private — the object's own ACL overrides for that object specifically, independent of the bucket's ACL.
